subdomain: 2.3 Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)

en.question: A team wants to certify engineering calculations by prompting Claude to reveal its complete private chain of thought. A reviewer would approve an answer whenever the returned reasoning looks thorough. The chosen model supports thinking and summarized thinking output. Which revision best distinguishes a useful prompting technique from an unsupported assurance claim?

options.text: Require reasoning inside XML thinking tags and treat that text as the complete internal computation.
options.note: Tags only organize generated text; they do not expose private internal reasoning. Some models can decline requests to put private reasoning into the response.

options.text: Approve answers whenever a thinking summary is present, because summary generation validates the calculation.
options.note: A summary describes reasoning but is not an independent correctness check. Its presence does not establish that the calculation or its assumptions are valid.

options.text: Disable thinking so that a step-by-step answer becomes an exact record of the model's internal process.
options.note: A generated explanation is not a guaranteed transcript of internal computation. Disabling thinking does not create that guarantee.

options.text: Use supported thinking and concise justifications, with independent checks of calculation assumptions and results.
options.note: Visible thinking is summarized rather than raw chain of thought. Verifiable evidence and checks support an assurance decision without relying on a supposedly complete internal trace.
